title: Yemen
subtitle: 1900–today · The Imamate, Two Republics, Unification and the War

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: An isolationist imamate, a republican north and a Marxist south, their 1990 union and the 1994 war, three decades of Ali Abdullah Saleh, and since 2014 a country split between the Houthi authority in Sanaa and the internationally recognised council in Aden

entries.label: Imam Yahya Hamid al-Din
entries.hint: When the Ottomans withdrew in 1918 Imam Yahya made North Yemen an isolated Zaydi theocracy, ruling by personal decree and holding tribal shaykhs' sons as hostages for good behaviour. He lost Najran, Jizan and most of Asir to Saudi Arabia in the 1934 war.
entries.note: the Treaty of Sanaa (1934, with Britain) and the Treaty of Taif (1934, with Saudi Arabia); Paul Dresch, 'A History of Modern Yemen' (2000).

entries.label: Imam Ahmad and the last years of the kingdom
entries.hint: Ahmad survived the 1948 coup that killed his father, moved the capital to Taʿizz, and opened cautiously to the wider world — arms from the Soviet bloc, a brief federation with Nasser's Egypt — while crushing every reform attempt. He died in his bed days before the revolution.
entries.note: Dresch (2000); Robert Stookey, 'Yemen: The Politics of the Yemen Arab Republic' (1978).

entries.label: Muhammad al-Badr, the last imam
entries.hint: Al-Badr reigned for barely a week before the 1962 coup; he escaped to the northern highlands and led the royalist side through eight years of civil war. The 1970 settlement recognised the republic but reconciled the royalists, and he went into exile.
entries.note: Dresch (2000); Edgar O'Ballance, 'The War in the Yemen' (1971).

entries.label: Abdullah al-Sallal
entries.hint: The colonel who proclaimed the Yemen Arab Republic on 26 September 1962 and ruled it as a client of Egypt through the civil war. He was deposed in 1967 as Egyptian troops withdrew after the Six-Day War.
entries.note: the YAR proclamation of 26 September 1962; Jesse Ferris, 'Nasser's Gamble' (2013).

entries.label: Al-Iryani, al-Hamdi and al-Ghashmi
entries.hint: The republic's civilian president Abdul Rahman al-Iryani reconciled with the royalists in 1970; Ibrahim al-Hamdi, a reformer who curbed the shaykhs and the Saudis, was assassinated in 1977; his successor Ahmad al-Ghashmi was killed in 1978 by a bomb in a briefcase from the south.
entries.note: Dresch (2000); the al-Hamdi assassination remains officially unsolved.

entries.label: The party chairmen of the PDRY
entries.hint: South Yemen — the Arab world's only Marxist state — churned through leaders violently: Qahtan al-Shaʿbi, then Salmin Rubaiʿ ʿAli (executed 1978), Abdul Fattah Ismail, Ali Nasir Muhammad, and Haydar al-Attas. The 1986 party bloodletting killed thousands in days.
entries.note: the constitutions of the PRSY (1967) and PDRY (1970); Fred Halliday, 'Revolution and Foreign Policy: The Case of South Yemen' (1990).

entries.label: Ali Abdullah Saleh takes power
entries.hint: An army officer of modest origin, Saleh became YAR president in 1978 after two of his predecessors were killed inside a year. He built a system of patronage, tribal balancing and the General People's Congress party that kept him in power for 33 years.
entries.note: the GPC founding (1982); Sarah Phillips, 'Yemen's Democracy Experiment in Regional Perspective' (2008).

entries.label: President Ali Abdullah Saleh, unified Yemen
entries.hint: Saleh led the 1990 unification, won the 1994 civil war against southern secession, and governed a nominal multiparty republic as a personal regime. He described ruling Yemen as 'dancing on the heads of snakes'; he resigned under the 2011 GCC Initiative with immunity.
entries.note: the 1991 constitution and its 1994 and 2001 amendments; the GCC Initiative and Implementation Mechanism (Riyadh, 23 November 2011).

entries.label: President Abdrabbuh Mansur Hadi
entries.hint: Saleh's vice-president, elected unopposed in February 2012 as the single transitional candidate. He oversaw the National Dialogue, was placed under house arrest by the Houthis in 2014, fled to Aden and then Riyadh in 2015, and handed power to a council in April 2022.
entries.note: the February 2012 presidential election (single candidate, ~65% turnout, Supreme Commission for Elections and Referendum); UN Security Council Resolution 2216 (2015).

entries.label: The Supreme Political Council in Sanaa
entries.hint: After seizing the capital in 2014, the Houthi movement (Ansar Allah) formed a Supreme Political Council in 2016, headed since then by Mahdi al-Mashat, running the de facto state over the north-west highlands and coast where most Yemenis live. It is recognised by no state as of early 2026.
entries.note: the Houthi–GPC 'Supreme Political Council' agreement (2016); UN Panel of Experts on Yemen annual reports.

entries.label: The Presidential Leadership Council in Aden
entries.hint: In April 2022 Hadi transferred his powers to an eight-member Presidential Leadership Council chaired by Rashad al-Alimi, folding in the Saudi- and UAE-backed factions. It is the internationally recognised government; as of early 2026 it is based mainly in Aden and Riyadh.
entries.note: Hadi's transfer decree of 7 April 2022; the Riyadh consultations; UN Security Council statements 2022–2025.

entries.label: The governments of the two Yemens and the union
entries.hint: The YAR's technocrat prime ministers — Muhsin al-Aini, Abdul Karim al-Iryani, Abdul Aziz Abdul Ghani — ran development on Saudi and Western aid, and after 1990 the unified cabinets, often GPC–Islah coalitions, managed IMF adjustment and a widening security crisis.
entries.note: the YAR and Republic of Yemen government gazettes; Phillips (2008).

entries.label: Wartime governments, in exile and in Sanaa
entries.hint: Since 2011 the recognised government — Basindwa, Bahah, Maeen Abdulmalik, Ahmed bin Mubarak — has governed mostly from Aden or Riyadh, while a parallel Houthi 'Government of Change and Construction' runs Sanaa. As of early 2026 there are two rival cabinets, ministries and gazettes.
entries.note: the rival government appointment decrees; the ministries' own communiqués; ACAPS and UN OCHA governance briefings.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The 1934 loss to Saudi Arabia, the 1948 regicide, the 1962–70 civil war with Egypt in it, the Aden insurgency, the inter-Yemeni wars, the 1986 and 1994 bloodlettings, the Saʿda wars, and the war that began in 2014

entries.label: The war of 1934 and the loss of the north
entries.hint: A short war over the disputed northern provinces ended with the Treaty of Taif: Yemen ceded Najran, Jizan and most of Asir to Saudi Arabia on a lease renewed every few years. The border was not finally settled until 2000, and the loss still rankles.
entries.note: the Treaty of Taif, 20 May 1934; the border fixed by the Treaty of Jeddah, 12 June 2000.

entries.label: The 1948 regicide and the al-Waziri coup
entries.hint: Reformist officers and the sayyid ʿAbd Allah al-Waziri assassinated Imam Yahya and declared a 'constitutional' imamate. Yahya's son Ahmad rallied the northern tribes, retook Sanaa within weeks, and let them sack it. Dozens of the plotters were executed.
entries.note: Dresch (2000); the 'Sacred National Pact' of the constitutionalists (1948).

entries.label: The civil war and Egypt's intervention
entries.hint: Republicans backed by up to 70,000 Egyptian troops fought royalists funded by Saudi Arabia and Jordan for eight years; Egypt used poison gas on royalist villages. The 1970 settlement kept the republic but absorbed the royalist leadership. Estimates of the dead run from 100,000 to 200,000.
entries.note: Ferris, 'Nasser's Gamble' (2013); O'Ballance (1971). Casualty figures are estimates and vary widely between sources.

entries.label: The Aden Emergency
entries.hint: An insurgency by the Egyptian-backed NLF and the FLOSY against British rule, with the two groups also fighting each other. Britain announced withdrawal in 1966 and left in November 1967; the NLF took over what became South Yemen.
entries.note: Jonathan Walker, 'Aden Insurgency' (2005); the British government White Paper on withdrawal (1966).

entries.label: The border wars of 1972 and 1979
entries.hint: The two Yemens twice went to war along their border, in 1972 and 1979, and each time signed a unity agreement in the aftermath that went nowhere. The wars hardened the division even as the rhetoric promised union.
entries.note: the Cairo Agreement (1972) and the Kuwait Agreement (1979); Halliday (1990).

entries.label: The events of January 1986
entries.hint: A politburo meeting turned into a massacre when President Ali Nasir Muhammad's guards opened fire on his rivals; ten days of street fighting in Aden followed. Estimates of the dead range from about 4,000 to 10,000; Ali Nasir fled north with tens of thousands of followers.
entries.note: Halliday, 'Revolution and Foreign Policy' (1990); the BBC and contemporary press. The death toll is disputed.

entries.label: The war of secession
entries.hint: Four years after unification the former southern leadership declared a breakaway 'Democratic Republic of Yemen'. Northern forces, with Islah militia and returned Afghan-war fighters, captured Aden in July 1994 after ten weeks. The south's sense of a northern conquest dates from here.
entries.note: Dresch (2000); Stephen Day, 'Regionalism and Rebellion in Yemen' (2012).

entries.label: Six rounds of war with the Houthis
entries.hint: Between 2004 and 2010 the Saleh government fought six rounds of war against the Houthi movement in and around Saʿda. The founder, Husayn al-Houthi, was killed in 2004; his brother Abdul-Malik took over. A 2009–10 round drew in the Saudi military along the border.
entries.note: the International Crisis Group reports on the Saʿda wars (2009–10); Barak Salmoni et al., 'Regime and Periphery in Northern Yemen' (RAND, 2010).

entries.label: The war since 2014
entries.hint: Houthi forces and Saleh loyalists seized Sanaa in September 2014 and advanced south; a Saudi-led coalition intervened in March 2015 with air power and a blockade. As of early 2026 the country is partitioned, a UN-mediated truce from April 2022 largely holds, and no settlement has been reached.
entries.note: UN Security Council Resolutions 2201, 2216 (2015) and 2624 (2022); the UN Special Envoy's briefings; ACLED and the Yemen Data Project for the conduct of the war.

entries.label: AQAP and the counterterrorism war
entries.hint: From the bombing of the USS Cole in Aden harbour in 2000, through the 2009 merger that created al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula, to AQAP's seizure of Mukalla in 2015–16, southern and eastern Yemen has been a base for the group and a target of a long US drone campaign.
entries.note: the FBI report on the USS Cole (2000); Gregory Johnsen, 'The Last Refuge' (2013); the New America and Long War Journal strike trackers.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The theocratic decree of the imamate, the merger of two legal systems in 1990, the Gulf-brokered transition of 2011, the split of the state's institutions after 2016, and the adjustment that brought bread riots

entries.label: The rule of the imam
entries.hint: Imam Yahya and then Ahmad governed by Zaydi law as interpreted by the imam and by personal fiat, with no written constitution, no political parties and no press. The state was the imam's household writ large, deliberately sealed off from the outside world.
entries.note: Dresch (2000); Manfred Wenner, 'Modern Yemen 1918–1966' (1967).

entries.label: Unification and the constitutions
entries.hint: The 1990 union merged the YAR's and PDRY's legal orders; a 1991 constitution, endorsed by referendum, established a multiparty republic. Amendments in 1994 and 2001 concentrated power in the presidency and lengthened its term — the legal track of Saleh's personal rule.
entries.note: the Constitution of the Republic of Yemen (1991) and its 1994 and 2001 amendments; the May 1991 constitutional referendum.

entries.label: The GCC Initiative and the National Dialogue
entries.hint: The Gulf-brokered deal that ended the 2011 crisis gave Saleh immunity and set up a transition: a consensus president, a unity government, and a ten-month National Dialogue Conference. Its federal plan of six regions was rejected by the Houthis and by southern delegates.
entries.note: the GCC Initiative and its Implementation Mechanism (23 November 2011); the National Dialogue Conference Final Document (January 2014).

entries.label: Two states inside one country
entries.hint: After 2016 the Central Bank was split between Aden and Sanaa, and the two zones developed rival ministries, courts, curricula, customs regimes and even banknotes. As of early 2026 a Yemeni's papers, currency and law depend on which side of the front line they live.
entries.note: the September 2016 relocation of the Central Bank to Aden; World Bank and ACAPS reports on the divided institutions.

entries.label: Structural adjustment and the 1998 bread riots
entries.hint: After the post-Gulf-War collapse, Yemen agreed an IMF and World Bank programme of subsidy cuts and a floated riyal. Price rises triggered deadly riots, worst in 1998, and left a lasting popular association of 'reform' with hardship imposed from outside.
entries.note: the IMF Article IV consultations 1995–98; Sheila Carapico, 'Civil Society in Yemen' (1998).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: A Zaydi revival that became an armed movement, Saudi-funded Salafism pushing into the highlands, the Islah party's political Islam, the Hadrami Sufi tradition under attack, and the end of Yemeni Jewry

entries.label: The Zaydi revival and the Houthi movement
entries.hint: The 'Believing Youth' study circles of 1990s Saʿda grew, under Husayn al-Houthi's teaching, into a Zaydi revivalist movement reacting to state neglect and Salafi encroachment. After 2004 it became Ansar Allah, an armed movement and then, from 2014, a governing power.
entries.note: Salmoni et al., 'Regime and Periphery in Northern Yemen' (RAND, 2010); Marieke Brandt, 'Tribes and Politics in Yemen: A History of the Houthi Conflict' (2017).

entries.label: Salafism moves into the highlands
entries.hint: From the 1980s, Saudi-funded Salafi teaching — above all Muqbil al-Wadiʿi's Dar al-Hadith institute at Dammaj, deep in Zaydi territory — spread a doctrine hostile to the Zaydi tradition. The two currents clashed, and Dammaj was besieged and closed by the Houthis in 2014.
entries.note: Bernard Haykel and Laurent Bonnefoy, 'Salafism in Yemen' (2011); Bonnefoy, 'Salafism in Yemen: Transnationalism and Religious Identity' (2011).

entries.label: Islah and the Muslim Brotherhood current
entries.hint: The Yemeni Congregation for Reform (al-Islah) — a coalition of the Muslim Brotherhood, tribal figures and Salafis — was Saleh's junior partner, then his opposition, and a leading force in the 2011 uprising. It has been targeted by the Houthis and, at times, by the UAE-backed south.
entries.note: Jillian Schwedler, 'Faith in Moderation: Islamist Parties in Jordan and Yemen' (2006).

entries.label: The Hadrami tradition under pressure
entries.hint: The ʿAlawi Sufi-legal tradition of Tarim, with its Dar al-Mustafa seminary and its global diaspora networks, has been targeted by both AQAP and Salafi currents while remaining the anchor of a distinct Hadrami identity increasingly at odds with Sanaa.
entries.note: Engseng Ho, 'The Graves of Tarim' (2006); reporting on AQAP attacks on Sufi sites in Hadramawt.

entries.label: The end of Yemeni Jewry
entries.hint: Operation Magic Carpet airlifted some 49,000 Jews to the new state of Israel in 1949–50; a remnant of a few hundred in the north dwindled under pressure, and the last identified Jewish families were removed from Houthi-controlled areas around 2021, ending a presence of over two thousand years.
entries.note: Tudor Parfitt, 'The Road to Redemption: The Jews of the Yemen 1900–1950' (1996); UN and press reporting on the departure of the last families, 2020–21.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The mud skyscrapers of old Sanʿaʾ and Shibam under airstrikes and floods, a modern literature of imamate and war, the recorded age of Sanʿani song, and the tower house as a badge of identity

entries.label: The old cities under war
entries.hint: Old Sanʿaʾ, the mud-brick towers of Shibam Hadramawt (a UNESCO site since 1982), and Zabid are all World Heritage; airstrikes, shelling, flooding and neglect since 2015 have damaged all three, and Zabid and Shibam sit on the danger list.
entries.note: UNESCO World Heritage Centre state-of-conservation reports on Yemen (2015–2024); the 2020 flood damage to Sanʿaʾ and Tarim.

entries.label: The modern Yemeni novel
entries.hint: Muhammad Abd al-Wali wrote the imamate's cruelties; Zayd Muti' Dammaj's 'The Hostage' (1984) fictionalised the shaykhs' hostage sons; Wajdi al-Ahdal, Ali al-Muqri and Bushra al-Maqtari have written the revolution and the war. It is a small literature carrying an outsized weight of testimony.
entries.note: Zayd Muti' Dammaj, al-Rahina (1984, tr. 'The Hostage'); Ali al-Muqri, 'The Handsome Jew' and 'Hurma'.

entries.label: The recorded age of Sanʿani song
entries.hint: Radio and record made stars of the ʿud masters — Ayyub Tarish, who composed the national anthem, Ahmad Fathi, the Adeni tradition, the singer Amina al-Sabri — and the classical Sanʿani repertoire now survives partly through recordings and diaspora performance.
entries.note: Jean Lambert, 'La médecine de l'âme' (1997); the UNESCO listing of 'the song of Sanʿaʾ' as intangible cultural heritage (2003).

entries.label: The tower house as national image
entries.hint: The multi-storey stone-and-brick house with its gypsum-traced qamariyya fanlights became, through tourism posters, banknotes and new construction, the visual shorthand for Yemen itself — a heritage style consciously deployed as identity.
entries.note: Michele Lamprakos, 'Building a World Heritage City: Sanaa, Yemen' (2015).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The reform pamphlets that fed the 1962 revolution, the contested national narratives of unity and 'occupation', the outside ethnography of Yemen, and the fraught project of counting the war's dead

entries.label: The Free Yemeni Movement
entries.loc: Aden and Cairo · aimed at Sanaa
entries.hint: Exiles in Aden and Cairo — Ahmad al-Zubayri, Ahmad Muhammad Nuʿman, the newspaper Sawt al-Yaman — built a written critique of the imamate as backward and tyrannical. It supplied the language and much of the leadership of the 1962 revolution.
entries.note: al-Zubayri and Nuʿman, 'Maṭalib al-shaʿb' (The Demands of the People); J. Leigh Douglas, 'The Free Yemeni Movement 1935–1962' (1987).

entries.label: Contested national narratives
entries.hint: 1962, 1967, 1990 and 1994 are each remembered incompatibly north and south — a unifying republican revolution against a story of a southern state annexed. The war since 2014 has added a Houthi narrative of a 'blessed step' against corruption and foreign control.
entries.note: Lisa Wedeen, 'Peripheral Visions: Publics, Power, and Performance in Yemen' (2008); Stephen Day, 'Regionalism and Rebellion in Yemen' (2012).

entries.label: The ethnography of Yemen
entries.hint: An unusually rich outside literature — Dresch on tribes, Weir on qat, Messick on law, vom Bruck on the sada, Wedeen on national feeling — has made Yemen a reference case in political anthropology and shapes how policymakers read it.
entries.note: Paul Dresch, 'Tribes, Government and History in Yemen' (1989); Shelagh Weir, 'A Tribal Order' (2007).

entries.label: Counting the war
entries.hint: The Yemen Data Project logs airstrikes, ACLED logs violent events, the UN Panel of Experts documents violations, and Mwatana for Human Rights records abuses by all sides. Every casualty total for the war is an estimate, and the parties dispute them.
entries.note: the Yemen Data Project; ACLED Yemen datasets; the UNDP report 'Assessing the Impact of War on Development in Yemen' (2019, 2021).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: An economy built on Gulf remittances and then wrecked by their loss, a short oil age, qat eating the water table, and since 2015 a halving of national income and a currency split in two

entries.label: Remittances and the 1990–91 expulsion
entries.loc: Yemen · and Saudi Arabia and the Gulf
entries.hint: For two decades Yemen ran on the wages sent home by its migrant workers in Saudi Arabia and the Gulf. After Yemen's stance during the 1990–91 Gulf crisis, Saudi Arabia expelled an estimated 800,000 to a million Yemeni workers, and remittances and Gulf aid collapsed.
entries.note: Nicholas Van Hear on the 1990–91 return migration; World Bank and IMF Yemen data for the remittance fall.

entries.label: The short oil and gas age
entries.loc: Marib and the Masila block, Yemen
entries.hint: Commercial oil from Marib in 1984 and the Hadramawt in the 1990s made both Yemens more viable and helped drive the 1990 union. Output peaked around 2001–03 near 450,000 barrels a day and then fell; the Balhaf LNG plant opened in 2009 and shut in 2015.
entries.note: the OPEC Annual Statistical Bulletin and EIA data for Yemen; the Balhaf force-majeure declaration (2015).

entries.label: Qat and the water table
entries.hint: By the 2000s qat took up a large share of the country's irrigated land and of household spending, and consumed a major fraction of the water pumped from Yemen's aquifers. It is simultaneously the biggest cash crop and the biggest driver of the water crisis.
entries.note: Shelagh Weir, 'Qat in Yemen: Consumption and Social Change' (2007); Gerhard Lichtenthäler on Yemeni water.

entries.label: Running out of water
entries.loc: Sanaa and the highland basins, Yemen
entries.hint: Diesel-pumped irrigation has drawn the highland aquifers down faster than they recharge; Sanʿaʾ has been described for years as one of the first capitals at risk of running dry. This is a structural crisis that predates the war and will outlast it.
entries.note: the World Bank 'Yemen: Assessing the Impacts of Climate Change and Variability on the Water and Agricultural Sectors' (2010); Christopher Ward, 'The Water Crisis in Yemen' (2015).

entries.label: The economy since 2015
entries.hint: The UN and World Bank estimate Yemen's economy has contracted by roughly half since 2015; the riyal has lost most of its value and trades at two different rates in the two zones, and public-sector salaries in the north went largely unpaid for years.
entries.note: World Bank 'Yemen Economic Monitor' series (2016–2025); UNDP (2019, 2021).

entries.label: The aid and blockade economy
entries.loc: Hodeida, Aden and the crossing points, Yemen
entries.hint: Import restrictions, port inspections and fuel blockades have made the movement of food and fuel a weapon; a UN-led aid operation has fed a large share of the population; and a war economy of levies, smuggling and profiteering has grown up around the fronts.
entries.note: the UN Verification and Inspection Mechanism (UNVIM); UN OCHA Humanitarian Needs Overviews for Yemen (2016–2025); the UN Panel of Experts on the war economy.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: An early and intensive drone-war theatre, later a producer of long-range missiles and drones of its own, and an infrastructure systematically degraded since 2015

entries.label: The drone and missile war
entries.loc: Yemen · and targets in Saudi Arabia, the UAE and the Red Sea
entries.hint: Yemen was one of the first countries hit by armed US drones, from 2002. Since the mid-2010s the Houthis have fielded their own drones and ballistic and cruise missiles, striking Saudi oil facilities in 2019, Abu Dhabi in 2022, and Red Sea shipping and Israel from 2023.
entries.note: the New America and Long War Journal strike trackers; the UN Panel of Experts on Houthi weapons systems; press reporting on the 2019 Abqaiq strike and the 2023–25 Red Sea attacks.

entries.label: Infrastructure and its destruction
entries.hint: Post-1970 aid built roads, a rebuilt Marib dam (1986, funded by the UAE), a national grid and the ports. Since 2015 airstrikes, shelling and lack of maintenance have wrecked much of it — bridges, water systems, power plants, Hodeida's cranes, Sanʿaʾ's airport.
entries.note: the World Bank 'Yemen Dynamic Needs Assessment' series (2016–2020); UNOSAT damage assessments.

entries.label: Communications under two authorities
entries.hint: Mobile phones and internet spread late and fast, then split with the country: the north's networks run from Sanʿaʾ, the south's from Aden, both used for surveillance. The system is also the pipe for remittances, banking and what independent journalism survives.
entries.note: Access Now and SMEX reporting on Yemen's internet; the 2022 nationwide outage after a strike on a Hodeida telecoms facility.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Egypt's costly intervention, a Cold War fault line down a divided nation, near-total dependence on Saudi Arabia, disputed Iranian support to the Houthis, and a Red Sea shipping crisis that returned Yemen to the world's front pages

entries.label: Egypt's intervention
entries.loc: Cairo · fighting in the Yemeni highlands
entries.hint: Nasser committed up to 70,000 troops to the Yemeni republic — 'Egypt's Vietnam' — for five years, tying down his army and treasury on the eve of the 1967 war with Israel. The withdrawal was one of the terms of the post-1967 Arab summit at Khartoum.
entries.note: Ferris, 'Nasser's Gamble: How Intervention in Yemen Caused the Six-Day War and the Decline of Egyptian Power' (2013).

entries.label: The Cold War fault line
entries.hint: South Yemen took Soviet and East German advisers, arms and a naval base at Aden; North Yemen took Saudi and American money and, at times, Soviet arms too. The one Cold War front line on the Arabian Peninsula ran between two halves of one nation.
entries.note: Halliday, 'Revolution and Foreign Policy: The Case of South Yemen 1967–1987' (1990).

entries.label: Saudi Arabia and Yemen
entries.hint: From the 1934 border to decades of direct payments to shaykhs, the 2000 Treaty of Jeddah, and the leadership of the coalition since 2015, Saudi Arabia has been the decisive external actor in Yemeni politics. The recognised government has depended on Riyadh for its survival and its budget.
entries.note: the Treaty of Jeddah (2000); F. Gregory Gause, 'Saudi-Yemeni Relations' (1990); the Saudi 'Special Committee' payments documented by the UN Panel of Experts.

entries.label: Iran and the Houthis
entries.hint: Iran has given Ansar Allah political backing and, from the mid-2010s, weapons technology and training; the coalition frames the movement as an Iranian proxy, the Houthis deny direction from Tehran, and independent assessments put the relationship somewhere between the two claims.
entries.note: the UN Panel of Experts on Yemen (2015–2025) on Iranian-origin weapons; Thomas Juneau, 'Iran's policy towards the Houthis in Yemen' (2016).

entries.label: The Red Sea crisis
entries.hint: From November 2023 the Houthis attacked commercial shipping in the Bab al-Mandab, declaring solidarity with Gaza; the US and UK struck Houthi targets from January 2024. Traffic through the Suez Canal fell sharply, and Yemen was again at the centre of a global crisis.
entries.note: IMB and UNCTAD data on Red Sea shipping and Suez traffic 2023–25; the US Central Command strike releases; press reporting on the May 2025 US–Houthi understanding on shipping.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: Two states then one, a union that four years later became a war, the humanitarian catastrophe the UN has called the world's worst, and a frozen conflict with no settlement

entries.label: Two states, one nation
entries.hint: For twenty-three years a Marxist People's Democratic Republic in the south and a tribal republic in the north faced each other across a fortified border, each calling itself Yemen and each backed by an opposing bloc.
entries.note: Dresch, 'A History of Modern Yemen' (2000); Halliday (1990).

entries.label: Union and its unravelling
entries.hint: The 1990 merger was quick and hopeful; the 1994 war four years later left the south feeling annexed rather than united. Every crisis since has been read in the south through the lens of that year.
entries.note: Day, 'Regionalism and Rebellion in Yemen' (2012).

entries.label: The world's worst humanitarian crisis
entries.hint: The UN has repeatedly called Yemen the largest humanitarian emergency of its time: the biggest cholera outbreak in recorded history (over 2.5 million suspected cases, 2016–21), mass hunger, and — by the UNDP's estimate — around 377,000 deaths from the conflict to the end of 2021, most from indirect causes. The figures are contested.
entries.note: WHO cholera situation reports for Yemen (2016–21); UNDP, 'Assessing the Impact of War on Development in Yemen' (2019, 2021); UN OCHA. Casualty estimates vary by source and method.

entries.label: A frozen war
entries.hint: The UN-mediated truce of April 2022 stopped most of the front-line fighting without producing a settlement. As of early 2026 Yemen remains divided between the Houthi authority in the north-west and the Presidential Leadership Council in the south, with talks stalled and the Red Sea crisis unresolved.
entries.note: the UN Special Envoy's Security Council briefings (2022–2025); the April 2022 truce and its lapsed formal renewal. This entry records the situation as of early 2026 and makes no prediction.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Women prominent in the 2011 uprising and then pushed out of the talks, the war's disproportionate toll on women and children, the Black underclass of the muhamashin, and a generation of child soldiers

entries.label: Tawakkol Karman and the women of 2011
entries.hint: The journalist and activist Tawakkol Karman shared the 2011 Nobel Peace Prize — the first Arab woman laureate — for her role in the uprising, in which women were highly visible organisers. Women held 28 percent of the National Dialogue seats and almost none in the talks since.
entries.note: the Norwegian Nobel Committee citation (2011); the National Dialogue Conference quota; UN Women reporting on the peace process.

entries.label: Women and the war
entries.hint: Maternal healthcare has collapsed, child marriage has risen as families seek dowries or protection, women make up a large share of the displaced, and women run much of the local aid response — while being almost entirely absent from the formal negotiations.
entries.note: UNFPA Yemen situation reports (2016–2025); Oxfam and CARE, 'From the Ground Up: Gender and Conflict Analysis in Yemen' (2016).

entries.label: The muhamashin
entries.loc: the Tihama and the city margins, Yemen
entries.hint: Yemen's Black underclass — the muhamashin, an estimated one to three million people, long called the derogatory 'Akhdam' — remains confined to the lowest work and the edges of towns, is heavily over-represented among the war's displaced and destitute, and has begun organising for civil rights.
entries.note: Marta Colburn and the Sana'a Center for Strategic Studies on the muhamashin; Minority Rights Group International profiles.

entries.label: A generation at war
entries.hint: The UN has verified the recruitment of thousands of children by all parties to the conflict, most by the Houthis. Two-thirds of Yemenis are under 25, millions of children have been out of school for years, and rates of malnutrition among the young are among the highest in the world.
entries.note: the UN Secretary-General's annual reports on Children and Armed Conflict (2016–2025); UNICEF Yemen situation reports.

events.l: The party chairmen of the PDRY
